telephone.intro: The simulator is a teaching model, not a reconstruction method. Its limits are real.

points.text: The simulation treats every scribe's errors as independent. Real scribes copied from exemplars inside text-families, so shared mistakes travel together and independent lines are fewer than the tree suggests.
The earliest generations, before about 150 AD, have almost no surviving witnesses. The tree is thinnest exactly where it matters most.
Majority vote is not how textual criticism works. Editors weigh witnesses by age, family and coherence (for example the CBGM), and sometimes follow a minority reading.
Some changes were deliberate (harmonizations, doctrinal clarifications), and deliberate changes are more likely to be copied than random slips.

timeline.intro: The chart shows access to earlier witnesses growing over time. What it does not show matters too.

points.text: Count is not the same as reliability. Most of the roughly 5,800 manuscripts are medieval, copied more than 800 years after the originals.
The first hundred years after composition still have very few witnesses, and papyrus dates rest on handwriting comparison, which some scholars think is less precise than usually presented.
The manuscript counts for other ancient authors come from older, uneven scholarship and change as catalogues are revised; comparisons between them are rough.
The figure of about 5,800 counts every catalogued item, including fragments of only a few verses and lectionaries.

p66.intro: P66 is an early and substantial witness to John. How early, and how careful, are debated.

points.text: P66 is usually dated about 200 AD, but some scholars argue for the 3rd or even 4th century on palaeographic grounds.
Its scribe made many mistakes and corrections, including singular readings found nowhere else. That shows careless copying at one point, and also careful checking at another; it cuts both ways.
points.source: Royse, Scribal Habits in Early Greek NT Papyri (2008)

variants.intro: The numbers here are real, and some of them are large.

points.text: There are roughly 400,000 textual variants among the Greek manuscripts, more variants than there are words in the New Testament. The app shows this number rather than hiding it.
A few variants are theologically interesting: the long ending of Mark and the Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7-8) were read as Scripture for centuries.
The category percentages are estimates from popular-level summaries, not a published count of every variant.

names.intro: The name statistics are suggestive. The sample is small and the method has critics.

points.text: The Gospels and Acts name only dozens of Palestinian Jews, not thousands, so percentages move a lot with each name.
Bauckham's own arithmetic and his choice of which names to count have been questioned.
points.source: 'Name Recall in the Synoptic Gospels', NTS 2022

points.text: A good match shows that the tradition came from 1st-century Palestine. It does not by itself show that eyewitnesses wrote the Gospels.

coincidences.intro: Undesigned coincidences are a cumulative argument, and each link can be challenged.

points.text: Some coincidences can be explained by literary dependence: Luke and Matthew knew Mark, so shared details are not always independent.
There is a selection effect: we notice the pieces that fit and ignore the details that do not interlock.
The narrower claim still stands: this kind of interlocking is uncommon in the apocryphal gospels, and that contrast is the actual argument.
